tldr: By adding a residual adapter that slightly modifies motion reference values from proprioception to a general motion tracker (GMT) trained on large-scale humanoid data, this work achieves safe and compliant whole-body control while preserving high motion tracking accuracy.
hero_caption: The overall training and deployment workflow of C-GMT. During training, the behavior of a privileged teacher—which generates compliant motion references using inverse kinematics (IK) from external forces and target stiffness—is distilled into a residual adapter that takes only a history of proprioception as input. During deployment, it produces compliant full-body responses simply by adding residuals to the reference tokens without force sensors.
overview:
To deploy humanoid robots in human living spaces, they must not only perform diverse, agile motions, but also exhibit compliance to prevent injuries and damage when contacting people or the environment. However, conventional motion tracking policies (General Motion Trackers, or GMTs) are trained to rigidly stick to commanded joint trajectories. When unexpected contact occurs, they try to force themselves back to the original pose, exerting excessive forces. Meanwhile, prior work on compliant control was either limited to single motions or could only respond compliantly in the upper body, making it difficult to achieve both generality and full-body compliance.

The authors focused on an intuitive idea: instead of altering the motion tracker itself, shift the target reference motion in real time based on external interaction forces. Specifically, they proposed Compliant GMT (C-GMT). It freezes a force-robust base motion tracker and adds on a lightweight residual adapter that predicts reference adjustments from a history of proprioception, such as joint angles.

Evaluation was conducted in simulation and on the real Unitree G1 robot across walking, dynamic dancing, teleoperation, and integration with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. As a result, C-GMT dramatically softened impact forces upon contact while matching the high tracking accuracy of stiff baseline trackers. Even under strong external disturbances, it coordinated its entire body to maintain balance and successfully complete tasks.
contributions: Achieving whole-body compliant control with a single policy for the first time by combining a residual adapter with the latent space of a general motion tracking policy.

Establishing a framework to efficiently train and distill a residual adapter operating solely on proprioception (internal sensors) from a privileged teacher using external force information and whole-body IK.
Devising two new Anti-Oscillation Losses to suppress unwanted joint vibrations that often arise during compliant motions.

Demonstrating on the real Unitree G1 robot contact avoidance during dynamic dancing, whole-body pushing/pulling during teleoperation, and substantial improvements in VLA task success rates under disturbance.

sections.heading: Why is humanoid 'stiff tracking' a problem, and how do we solve it?
sections.summary: Motion trackers trained on large-scale motion capture data reproduce diverse motions with high fidelity, but they remain stiff during contact, posing safety risks. Prior work suffered from a trade-off between generality and compliance. This paper successfully achieves both via a residual adapter that adapts reference trajectories.
sections.details:
When bringing humanoid robots into human society, balancing diverse and agile motor performance with compliant safety during contact with humans or the environment is a core challenge. In recent humanoid control, general motion trackers (GMTs) trained via imitation learning on large-scale human motion capture (MoCap) data have become the standard approach. However, conventional GMTs are trained as stiff controllers that forcefully reject disturbances. When physical contact occurs, they aggressively fight to return to the original trajectory, generating excessive contact forces that risk damaging the robot and its surroundings.

While compliant control has been studied to address this problem, existing methods that yield coordinated whole-body compliant responses have been restricted to single motions such as standing. Conversely, those that track general motions could only respond compliantly with their upper bodies. Trying to teach a single neural network motion tracking, balance maintenance, force estimation, and compliant response all at once from scratch leads to massive training times and extremely difficult reward design.

The key insight here is a division of labor between a robust, disturbance-resistant motion tracker and a residual adapter that compliantly shifts the target motion. By designing an analytical teacher (privileged teacher) that generates reference trajectories based on external forces, and distilling its behavior into an adapter predicting from proprioception (joint position and velocity history), the authors achieved both high-precision general motion tracking and whole-body compliance in a single model.

sections.heading: The limits of existing tracking and compliant control, and the strength of residuals
sections.summary: Conventional general trackers produce overly stiff contact behavior, while existing RL-based compliant controllers sacrifice generality. C-GMT gets the best of both worlds by freezing an existing tracker and applying residual adaptations to upstream motion references.
sections.details:
### II-A General Motion Tracking
Thanks to advances in reinforcement learning and Sim-to-Real techniques, general motion trackers (GMTs) that replay diverse movements from MoCap data have rapidly advanced. GMTs are widely used as execution engines for teleoperation and low-level motion executors for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing GMTs perform stiff position tracking. If a high-level planner has latency or errors, or if unexpected contact occurs, they produce uncontrollably high torques.

### II-B Learned Compliant Humanoid Control
Impedance control, which models the robot as a spring-mass-damper system to generate trajectories matching external forces, is classical, but balancing it with fall prevention on bipedal robots is extremely difficult. Prior works like GentleHumanoid and CHIP handle general tracking but restrict compliant responses to the upper body. SoftMimic achieves whole-body coordinated compliance, but requires training a separate policy from scratch for every single motion. C-GMT achieves both whole-body coordinated compliance and general tracking across arbitrary motions for the first time.

### II-C Residual Models for Humanoid Robotics
Residual learning is an attractive approach to extend functionality without destroying a base pretrained GMT. Prior work has used privileged information distillation from joint position and velocity histories to estimate environmental properties without external force sensors. C-GMT follows this direction by adopting a lightweight adapter that predicts residuals added to target motion tokens from proprioceptive history.

sections.heading: How C-GMT works: Privileged teacher, latent token adaptation, and anti-oscillation losses
sections.summary: The authors pre-tune a robust base tracker to withstand external force loads, then distill a privileged teacher based on spring laws and whole-body IK into a lightweight residual adapter fed by proprioception. They also introduce two new loss functions to suppress unwanted joint vibrations during compliant responses.
sections.details:
### III-A Force-Robust General Motion Tracker
The authors adopted SONIC as the base motion tracker, which represents motions quantized into discrete latent tokens using Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ). Since original SONIC does not account for sustained arm loads, they fine-tuned its decoder through curriculum learning, applying end-effector weights up to $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ and sustained forces of $10$ to $30\,\mathrm{N}$. By introducing an external force budget scale $\mu_c$ that automatically adjusts forces for clips with high failure rates, they prevented learning collapse in challenging poses and created a robust tracker that maintains specified postures even under heavy loads.

### III-B Compliant Teacher and Feasibility Tuning
From the ground-truth external force $\mathbf{F}_i$ applied to the hand and the commanded stiffness $K_t^{\mathrm{cmd}}$, target end-effector displacements are computed via Hooke's law: $\Delta \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{F}_i / K_t^{\mathrm{cmd}}$. They then solve a quadratic programming (QP) based whole-body inverse kinematics (IK) problem prioritizing foot placement and center of mass (CoM) control. This analytically yields whole-body postures that yield to external forces without falling. A simulation sweep over 4,096 motion clips and 8 force directions identified safe force limits beforehand to prevent the robot from falling.

### III-C Residual Adapter Architecture
The adapter is a lightweight MLP receiving a 10-step proprioceptive history (about 0.2 seconds), the current motion token $z$, and the log commanded stiffness $\log k$. To prevent jitter from crossing quantization boundaries, the residual correction $\Delta z$ is added directly after FSQ quantization. It also features a gating mechanism to easily output zero when there are no external forces, a deadband (threshold $0.005$) to cut tiny fluctuations, and an auxiliary head to estimate hand forces.

### III-D Residual Adapter Training & Anti-Oscillation Loss
The adapter is distilled to imitate the privileged teacher's output actions and tokens. It uses teacher trajectories early in training and transitions to student-driven trajectories containing the student's own prediction errors later on, making it robust to covariate shift.
A major hurdle was that joints tended to exhibit fine oscillations during compliant responses. Simple smoothness penalties hurt compliance, so the authors introduced two Anti-Oscillation Losses that penalize correlation between changes in joint velocity and changes in residual actions. Combining an unnormalized loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{osc}}$ to suppress dynamic, large-amplitude oscillations with a normalized, 5-step-interval loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{norm\_osc}}$ to catch micro-jitters near rest achieved both compliant yielding and crisp, stable settling.

captions.F2: The C-GMT architecture and training pipeline. The privileged teacher generates compliant reference motions using IK from true external forces and stiffness commands. The student residual adapter learns these modifications from proprioceptive history alone. At deployment, compliance is achieved simply by plugging in the adapter while keeping the base tracker frozen.

sections.heading: Verified on G1 and in simulation: Accurate stiffness, reduced contact in dynamic dance, and whole-body coordination
sections.summary: C-GMT accurately tracked commanded stiffness levels without compromising tracking accuracy during unperturbed motions. It halved collision forces during dance motions near a wall, coordinated whole-body crouching when hands were pulled down, and significantly boosted VLA task success rates under disturbance in both simulation and the real robot.
sections.details:
### IV-A C-GMT accurately tracks compliance levels
Applying forces to the hands in a standing posture, effective stiffness was measured from resulting displacements across commanded stiffnesses ($40$ to $600\,\mathrm{N/m}$). C-GMT showed an excellent linear relationship with commands across the entire range, matching the compliance accuracy of SoftMimic, which is trained specifically on standing alone.

### IV-B C-GMT is an accurate general motion tracker
In the absence of external forces, tracking performance was evaluated on the LAFAN1 dataset (12 locomotion clips and 17 dynamic clips). C-GMT maintained local tracking accuracy comparable to original SONIC (MPJPE around $17\,\mathrm{mm}$) and achieved a 100% success rate on dynamic clips, vastly outperforming TWIST2 and GentleHumanoid. Tracking accuracy remained nearly constant when varying stiffness from $k=100$ to $k=300$, showing that the adapter correctly distinguishes the robot's own motions from external contact.

### IV-C C-GMT enables safe interaction during dynamic motions
In an experiment where the robot replayed intense dance motions right beside a wall, baseline SONIC hit the wall hard and rebounded, while TWIST2 was thrown back with impact forces exceeding $250\,\mathrm{N}$. In contrast, C-GMT ($k=60\,\mathrm{N/m}$) compliantly retracted its hand upon detecting contact, keeping contact forces under roughly $50\,\mathrm{N}$ while continuing its dance. On the real G1 robot, when humans pulled its arm or when it bumped into a wall during dynamic dancing, it safely absorbed the forces without falling.

### IV-D C-GMT is robust to external disturbances
- **Whole-body coordinated bracing**: When hands were pulled strongly downward, GentleHumanoid (which only has upper-body compliance) could not bend its knees and fell at $110\,\mathrm{N}$. In contrast, C-GMT bent its knees deeply into a squat, similar to SoftMimic, distributing the load across its entire body to endure the disturbance.
- **Teleoperation and VLA robustness**: In real-robot teleoperation, it smoothly handled tasks like turning doorknobs to open doors, wiping whiteboards, and dragging chairs, even though the operator could not feel subtle contact forces. In integration experiments with a VLA model (GR00T) trained to lift boxes, SONIC stumbled and collided with the box under a $60\,\mathrm{N}$ lateral pull disturbance, failing the task. C-GMT yielded compliantly to the force, adjusted its footsteps, recovered, and successfully lifted the box.

captions.F4: Comparison of contact forces (a) and post-collision postures (b) during dynamic dance replay near a wall. TWIST2 generates impacts over 250N and gets thrown back, and SONIC pushes back hard. C-GMT keeps contact forces low, safely continuing tracking along the wall.
captions.F6: Comparison of lower-body coordination when hands are pulled downward. GentleHumanoid, which is compliant only in the upper body, fails to bend its knees and topples at 110N. C-GMT and SoftMimic squat by bending their knees, absorbing forces across the whole body to maintain stability.
captions.F7: Contact-rich teleoperation on the real Unitree G1 robot. Tasks like turning doorknobs to open doors, wiping whiteboards, dragging chairs while walking, and hugging a balance ball are executed stably as the adapter absorbs discrepancies even without operator haptic feedback.
captions.F8: Disturbance comparison during a box carrying task with VLA (GR00T). SONIC fights the disturbance, stumbles forward, knocks the box away, and fails. C-GMT yields compliantly to the external force, regains its balance, and successfully picks up the box.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: C-GMT is a modular framework that brings whole-body compliance to existing general trackers. Future work includes expanding contact adaptation beyond hands to arbitrary links and enabling high-level policies to adjust stiffness automatically.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Compliant GMT (C-GMT), which pairs a pretrained general motion tracker with residual reference adaptation to achieve both high-fidelity motion tracking and whole-body coordinated compliance. It breaks through the conventional trade-off of being limited to a single motion or having only upper-body compliance, demonstrating that humanoids can safely deflect forces even during dynamic motions. Moreover, it exhibits valuable practical benefits, such as improving teleoperation usability and boosting the disturbance tolerance of VLA tasks.

For future work, the current setup primarily focuses on disturbances at the hands (wrists). Extending this to contacts across arbitrary links on the entire body, such as knees or the back, remains an important next step. Furthermore, commanded stiffness $k$ is currently set manually by humans. In the future, high-level vision and language models are expected to autonomously determine and adjust optimal stiffness depending on task requirements and environmental context.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation and training hyperparameter details
sections.summary: Details the two-stage training setup using Isaac Lab and mjlab, whole-body IK weight distributions, network architectures, and real-world deployment techniques such as reference motion pausing under sudden force surges.
sections.details:
### A-A & A-B Force-Robust Tracker and Privileged Teacher Setup
The robust tracker was trained in Isaac Lab on the BONES-SEED dataset using three H200 GPUs for 5 days. Hand forces updated in direction and magnitude every 2 to 4 seconds, with the allowable force budget scaling gradually from $10\,\mathrm{N}$ to $30\,\mathrm{N}$. The privileged teacher's whole-body IK solves a quadratic program with tracking weights of 10.0 for end-effector displacement, 10.0 for foot placement, 5.0 for CoM maintenance, and 0.1 for nominal posture regularization.

### A-C & A-D Residual Adapter Architecture and Training Parameters
The adapter is an MLP with hidden layers $[512, 256]$ using ELU activations. The residual head uses tanh initialized to zero, preventing disturbances to the base tracker's behavior early in training. Training was conducted in mjlab (MuJoCo-Warp) using four H100 GPUs for 2 days of distillation. Forces up to $140\,\mathrm{N}$ and stiffnesses from $40$ to $600\,\mathrm{N/m}$ were sampled log-uniformly.

### A-E Deployment Strategies on Real Hardware (Safety Pause Logic)
For real-world control of the Unitree G1, an RTX 3080 laptop executed the adapter and GMT synchronously at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$. To prevent instability from unexpected interactions under excessive loads during motion replay, a practical failsafe pauses reference motion progression whenever the exponential moving average (EMA) of estimated external force exceeds a stiffness-dependent threshold, automatically resuming once the force subsides.

takeaways: Instead of training a motion tracking policy to be compliant from scratch, decoupling the system into a robust tracker plus latent residual reference adaptation achieves both training stability and broad generality.

Designing a privileged teacher with whole-body IK and spring laws allows physical feasibility to be verified beforehand in simulation and safely distilled into a student model that relies only on internal sensors.

High-frequency oscillations and micro-jitters inherent in compliant control can be effectively suppressed by two Anti-Oscillation Losses that penalize correlations between residual action changes and joint velocity changes.
Providing whole-body compliance in low-level controllers improves contact tolerance for high-level teleoperation and VLA models, significantly boosting real-world task success rates.
limitations: The system is primarily designed and validated for external forces acting on the hands (wrists); adaptation to direct contacts on the torso or legs remains limited.
The target stiffness parameter ($k$) must be manually provided externally, leaving autonomous adjustment based on task and environmental context to future high-level policies.
Compliant yielding under strong forces relies heavily on the IK formulation (prioritizing CoM and foot placement), and fall recovery via stepping is not yet integrated.
